unit.title: Computational thinking, unplugged and with blocks

video.title: Loops: Repeat the pattern
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: My robot needed twelve cards to walk round the playground square: forward, forward, forward, turn, again and again. Then a pupil said: Miss, it’s the same thing four times! She had just discovered loops.
Today: loops, and how they make programs shorter.
Look at the robot’s program. Forward three times, then turn right. Then the same again, and again, and again. When steps repeat, there is a pattern, and a pattern can become a loop.
A loop repeats a block of steps a number of times, or until something happens. Instead of twelve cards, you write: repeat four times, forward three, turn right. Four cards do the work of twelve.
Loops make programs shorter, but that is not the best part. Want a bigger square? Change one number, not twelve cards. Fewer cards means fewer places for a bug to hide.

Children already know loops. A song’s chorus comes back after every verse. A clapping game repeats the same pattern. A dance says: step, step, clap, four times. Writing it once and saying how many times is exactly what a loop does.
Quick check! My program is six forward cards in a row. If one card can repeat up to four times, how few cards can do the same walk?
Two cards: forward four times, then forward twice. One card can’t do six, because a card repeats at most four times. Limits like this make pupils think, and that’s the point.

Later, the same idea becomes code. In Python, a loop starts with for, and the lines inside it are pushed in from the edge. This one walks the whole square. The robot cards and the code are the same thinking.
Before running a loop, ask pupils to predict. How many squares will the robot walk? Where will it stop, and which way will it face? Predicting first turns guessing into thinking.
In the app, open Program a robot and try grids four to six. Tap a card in your program to repeat it. Then go for three stars: the fewest cards possible.
Your turn. My robot runs: repeat three times, forward two. How many squares does it move?
Six. Remember: repeated steps are a pattern. A loop repeats a block a number of times. It makes programs shorter and easier to change. And pupils already know loops from songs and games.
Try it in class tomorrow: dance loops. Groups invent a short dance, write it as a program with repeat, and swap programs. Can another group perform it exactly from the paper?

checkpoints.prompt: Six forward cards in a row; a card repeats up to 4 times. Fewest cards for the same walk?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — forward ×4, then forward ×2: two cards.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a card repeats at most 4 times, so it takes two: four, then two.

checkpoints.prompt: Repeat 3 times: forward 2. How many squares does the robot move?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — two squares, three times: six.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the loop repeats forward 2 three times: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
